The above forecast involved predicting the solution to a problem by human-AI collaboration. Fix an existing concrete mathematical research program (individual problem, or a smaller collection of problems). The difficulty of a research program can be measured by how long it would have postponed the solution of the Millennium Prize Problems. Take the research program of Littlewood-Offord problem, adapted to the bounds $[0,1]$ for the inner product. The goal is to study $M(\mathcal{A},u)$, the median of a set of linear functionals over Hamel bases, without relying on approximation by random subsets, because of the requirement for deterministic arithmetic progressions. The naïve homogeneous extension would have been to study $M(\mathcal{A},u,v) = P(M(\cal{A},u) > M(\cal{A},v))$. Semi-naïve, a cheap extension on the original would be to allow $h$ as an additional variable and impose bounds on the absolute value and expectation of $M(\cal{A},h)$. The precise formulation is left to your discretion. The research program should contain scope for AI contributions, in one direction or another. If feasible, the difficulty of the research program should be comparable to the Millennium Prize Problems (not an exact requirement).
